scenes.title: How attention works
scenes.narration: The animal crossed the street because it was tired. What does it refer to? You probably chose the animal. But change tired to wide, and the street becomes a better answer. The word it stayed the same. Its meaning changed with the words around it. This is the problem at the heart of the Transformer: how can a machine build a representation of a word that reflects its context?

scenes.title: Queries, keys & values
scenes.narration: Imagine reading the sentence from the position of it. The model makes a query for that position and a key for every position in the sentence. Comparing the query with each key gives a score. A bigger score means a stronger connection. The model then blends information, called values, using those connections as weights. The highlighted line illustrates one possible connection. It is an example, not a measurement from the paper.

scenes.title: Many heads, one layer
scenes.narration: One set of connections gives you one view of the sentence. A Transformer builds several views at once. Each attention head has different learned settings, so different heads can emphasize different relationships. The model combines their outputs into a new representation for each word. It also adds information about position. Otherwise, attention would have no way to tell whether animal came before street or after it.

scenes.title: What changed
scenes.narration: Why did this matter for translation? A recurrent encoder passes information from one position to the next. Attention lets distant words interact within a single layer, and an encoder can update all positions together. In the paper's English-to-German experiment, the Transformer reached 28.4 BLEU, a translation quality score. There are trade-offs. Standard attention compares every pair of positions, and the decoder still generates the translation one word at a time. The advance was changing how context is computed.

paper.title: Attention Is All You Need
sections: The animal crossed the street because it was tired. What does it refer to? You probably chose the animal. But change tired to wide, and the street becomes a better answer. The word it stayed the same. Its meaning changed with the words around it. This is the problem at the heart of the Transformer: how can a machine build a representation of a word that reflects its context?

Imagine reading the sentence from the position of it. The model makes a query for that position and a key for every position in the sentence. Comparing the query with each key gives a score. A bigger score means a stronger connection. The model then blends information, called values, using those connections as weights. The highlighted line illustrates one possible connection. It is an example, not a measurement from the paper.

One set of connections gives you one view of the sentence. A Transformer builds several views at once. Each attention head has different learned settings, so different heads can emphasize different relationships. The model combines their outputs into a new representation for each word. It also adds information about position. Otherwise, attention would have no way to tell whether animal came before street or after it.

Why did this matter for translation? A recurrent encoder passes information from one position to the next. Attention lets distant words interact within a single layer, and an encoder can update all positions together. In the paper's English-to-German experiment, the Transformer reached 28.4 BLEU, a translation quality score. There are trade-offs. Standard attention compares every pair of positions, and the decoder still generates the translation one word at a time. The advance was changing how context is computed.
